newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Hamas mounts Gaza rally with Arafat's blessing.
newsitem.headline: Hamas mounts Gaza rally with Arafat's blessing.

text.p: Thousands of supporters of the Islamic militant group Hamas staged a show of strength on Friday in self-ruled Gaza at a rally held with the blessing of Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.

Dozens of PLO paramilitary troops secured rooftops and streets around Khan Younis stadium in southern Gaza for the rally, Hamas's first since Israel and the Palestinian Authority cracked down on the group for launching a wave of suicide bomb attacks which killed scores in the Jewish state nine months ago.
Earlier Hamas' armed wing, hit hard by the crackdowns, said it would mark the first anniversary of the January killing of its master bombmaker by renewing attacks against Israel.
"This huge attendance confirms that Hamas is alive and will never die," Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh told the overflow rally crowd organisers put at some 20,000.
Hamas activists said the rally would have been even bigger had the PLO allowed it to take place in more populous Gaza City.

In a sign of unprecedented deference to the PLO -- which Hamas had reviled for signing peace deals with Israel the group denounced as surrender -- photos of Arafat hung alongside murals of slain Hamas fighters and bombmakers.
"We worship God by killing Jews," was the caption of a sign showing a bombed-out Israeli bus.

Hours earlier, Hamas's Izz el-Deen al-Qassam guerrilla wing said it was preparing for "military operations" to mark the death of bombmaker Yahya Ayyash, killed last January 5 in Gaza when a booby-trapped cellular telephone exploded. Israel was widely believed to have been behind the assassination.
Qassam responded with suicide bombings in February and March that killed 59 people in Israel.
In a statement faxed to an international news agency, Qassam promised a "strong, very painful ... major challenge" against Israeli targets.
The strident militarism typical of the group's rallies was also in evidence on Friday. One mural depicted a masked Hamas man knifing an Israeli soldier he held in a chokehold.
But Hamas sounded a note of accommodation with the Palestinian Authority.

"We are for political pluralism and freedom of expression," Abd al-Fattah Dukhan, a Hamas founder and spiritual leader, told the rally in a statement aimed at bringing the group back from the Palestinian political wilderness.
Hamas, which boycotted Palestinian elections last January for fear its participation would lend legitimacy to the PLO's peace deals, said it would soon open a political office in Gaza.

"This does not mean that we are cancelling our policy. It's just an administrative step in order to intensify the existence of Hamas and to establish its political activity through an official way," Hamas spokesman Mahmoud Zahhar told reporters.

Zahhar stressed Hamas's continued opposition to Israeli-PLO peace accords and reserved the right to undertake guerrilla attacks "as long as Israel continued its practices against the Palestinian people."
But he conceded the group's military activities could backfire and said strengthening the group's charitable and educational activities was equally critical for Palestinians.

Israel clamped a crippling closure on the West Bank and Gaza Strip after the wave of Hamas suicide attacks earlier this year. The closure, which has since been slightly eased, severely damaged the Palestinian economy.
Citing a Hamas victory in student elections at the West Bank's An-Najah University this week, Zahhar said the movement remained strong despite efforts to curb its operations.
"Hamas is a part of this land and no one can eradicate it."
